title: Least restrictive practice, searches and ward safety
blurb: Avoid blanket restrictions, search lawfully and respectfully, manage ligature risk and support positive risk-taking.
question: After one patient self-harmed with a phone charger cable, a ward manager proposes removing every patient's mobile phone and charger. A staff nurse is asked for her view. What is the best response?

teach.body: The first guiding principle of the MHA Code is the least restrictive option and maximising independence. Any restriction must be a proportionate response to an individually identified risk, applied for no longer than necessary and never to punish or humiliate. In plain English: restrict the person who needs it, as little as you can, for as short a time as you can, and write down why.
teach.cite: MHA Code of Practice 2015, ch1 and 8.5-8.9

teach.body: A blanket restriction is a rule or policy that restricts liberty or other rights, applied routinely to all patients, a class of patients or a whole service without individual risk assessment. Examples in the Code: banning mobile phones or chargers, limiting internet, mail, visiting hours, money or preferred activities. These should be avoided unless justified as necessary and proportionate for particular individuals, and need express authorisation by the hospital managers.

teach.caption: A blanket locked door can amount to a restriction or a deprivation of liberty for informal patients (COP15 8.10-8.11).

steps.label: Policy summary and consent
steps.sub: Say they do not have to consent (8.33-8.34; NG10 1.3.4)

steps.label: Record and receipt
steps.sub: What, why, how; items stored and returned (8.37, 8.45)

teach.h: A detained patient refuses a search

root.label: Refuses or lacks capacity to consent
root.sub: Keep separate and under close observation; explain

children.label: Contact the RC first
children.sub: Any clinical objection? MDT review before force (8.40; NG10 1.3.5)

teach.caption: After any search without consent: post-incident review and support for patient and staff (8.43-8.44; NG10 1.3.6).

head: Area
What good practice looks like
rows: Regular ligature risk assessment; most suicides on the ward are by hanging or strangulation
Consider removing, with the person involved (NG225 1.12.6)
Autonomy vs restriction; least restrictive measures (NG225 1.12.5)
Visible and accessible, especially at handover (NG225 1.12.4)
Make the person safe now, then report and fix
teach.caption: Source: NCISH; NICE NG225 1.12.

teach.body: Risk aversion has its own harms: lost skills, dependency, frustration and longer admissions. Therapeutic risk-taking means planning, with the person and the team, an activity that carries some risk because it supports recovery. For people who have self-harmed, NICE NG225 says it should follow a psychosocial assessment, draw on the person's strengths and coping strategies, focus on positive outcomes and be revisited as part of ongoing assessment.

Staff Nurse Kaur explains that a ward-wide phone ban is a blanket restriction the Code names as having no basis in best practice; it would cut every patient off from family and could breach Article 8. Instead she suggests reviewing the patient who self-harmed, agreeing with him how his charger is kept and used, recording the reason in his notes and reviewing it. Other patients keep their phones.

teach.text: Do not confuse 'it would be safer' with 'it is justified'. Locking the lounge because the ward is short-staffed, or searching everyone after one incident, are restrictions driven by staff convenience, not individual risk. Low staffing is never a reason for seclusion either (COP15 26.107).

items: Least restrictive option and maximising independence is the first Code principle.
Blanket restrictions are avoided unless necessary and proportionate, and need managers' authorisation.
Searches: proportionate, consent sought, two staff with one same sex, explained, recorded, receipt given.
Refused search: contact the RC, MDT review before force, unless there is an immediate danger.
Assess ligature and environmental risk; plan therapeutic risk-taking after psychosocial assessment.

summary: You can now tell an individual, proportionate restriction from a blanket one and carry out searches lawfully and respectfully. You can also manage ward environmental risk and support planned therapeutic risk-taking.

A.q: Which is an example of a blanket restriction under the MHA Code?
options: Removing a belt from one patient at high ligature risk
Setting the same visiting hours for every patient
Searching a patient suspected of hiding a blade
Escorting one patient on leave after an assault
A.why: COP15 8.5 and 8.7: rules applied to all patients without individual risk assessment, including visiting hours, are blanket restrictions.

whyNot.0: This is an individual restriction based on that person's assessed risk.
whyNot.2: A search based on a specific suspicion is an individual, proportionate response.
whyNot.3: This is tailored to one person's identified risk.

A.q: Under NICE NG10, who should carry out a personal search of a service user?
options: One nurse of the same sex
Two staff, both of the opposite sex
One nurse with a security officer
Two staff, at least one the same sex
A.why: NG10 1.3.3: searches are undertaken by 2 members of staff, at least 1 of whom is the same sex as the person being searched.

whyNot.0: NG10 requires two members of staff.
whyNot.1: At least one searcher should be the same sex as the person.
whyNot.2: NG10 specifies two staff with one the same sex, not a security officer.

A.q: What should staff tell a patient before asking to search their belongings, according to the MHA Code?
options: That refusing will lead to a loss of leave
That they do not have to consent
That the search is routine for all patients
That the police will be called if they refuse
A.why: COP15 8.34: a person to be searched should be told they do not have to consent; consent obtained by threat, intimidation or inducement is likely to make the search illegal.

whyNot.0: This is a threat that invalidates consent.
whyNot.2: Routine searching without cause is for exceptional circumstances only; it should not be implied.

B.q: Jake, 23, detained under section 3, refuses a search of his bag. Staff believe it contains cannabis but there is no sign of a weapon or immediate risk. What should happen next?
options: Search the bag by force straight away
Contact his RC and hold an MDT review
Return his bag and take no further action
Call the police to search him instead
B.why: COP15 8.40 and NG10 1.3.5: if a detained patient refuses, contact the RC without delay for any clinical objection and carry out a multidisciplinary review before using force, while keeping him separate and observed.

whyNot.0: Force without delay is for suspected immediate danger, which is absent here.
whyNot.2: The concern still needs a proportionate response and review.
whyNot.3: Police involvement is not the first step for a clinical search refusal.

B.q: After a search, staff remove a lighter and two razors from Maria's room. What does the MHA Code require?
options: Dispose of the items without telling her why
Return the items to her on the day she is discharged
Keep them in the office without making a record
Explain why, give a receipt and say when returned
B.why: COP15 8.45: tell the patient why items were removed, give a receipt, say where they are stored and when they will be returned; 8.37 requires a full record.

whyNot.0: Disposing without explanation breaches the Code's transparency requirements.
whyNot.1: Return should be set by review of risk, and she must be told this with a receipt.
whyNot.2: Every search and removal must be recorded.

B.q: On a short-staffed Sunday, the nurse in charge suggests locking the communal lounge so fewer areas need watching. What is the best response?
options: Advise against it, as it restricts all for staffing
Agree, if patients are told why it is locked
Agree, as it is temporary and helps safety
Advise locking bedrooms as well for consistency
B.why: COP15 8.5-8.6: restrictions must respond to individually identified risk, not be applied to everyone for staff convenience; this would be an unauthorised blanket restriction.

whyNot.1: Explaining a blanket restriction does not make it proportionate.
whyNot.2: Being temporary does not justify a restriction driven by staffing rather than risk.
whyNot.3: Extending it to bedrooms widens an unjustified restriction.

C.q: During an environmental check, a nurse finds a new wardrobe with an exposed hanging rail in the room of Kai, 20, who recently tried to hang himself. What should she do first?
options: Report it at the next ward safety meeting
Ask Kai to avoid using the wardrobe
Move Kai to safety now, then report it
Remove the wardrobe rail herself with tools
C.why: Most in-patient suicides on the ward are by hanging or strangulation (NCISH 2026: 91% of ward deaths). Immediate safety comes first: move Kai or increase observation, then report the ligature point so it is fixed and risk-assessed.

whyNot.0: Delaying leaves a known ligature point with a high-risk patient.
whyNot.1: Relying on Kai to avoid it does not manage a serious immediate risk.
whyNot.3: Improvised removal may create new hazards and bypasses estates and reporting.

C.q: Sanjay, 45, detained under section 3, is recovering from psychosis. He asks for escorted leave to attend a job interview, which carries some risk of stress. Which approach best reflects therapeutic risk-taking?
options: Refuse until he is ready for discharge from hospital
Plan it with him, the team and a contingency
Allow it and leave all of the planning to him
Delay until his risk scale score falls
C.why: COP15 1.5, 1.7 and 1.16: restrictions are the minimum necessary, care is planned with the patient, and care plans focus on recovery and positive outcomes. Therapeutic risk-taking means planning the leave with him and the team, building on his strengths, with a contingency if warning signs appear.

whyNot.0: Blanket refusal is risk aversion and works against recovery.
whyNot.2: Leaving planning to him alone ignores the team process and safety planning.
whyNot.3: Leave decisions rest on individual clinical assessment and planning with him, not on waiting for a scale score to fall.

C.q: Stella, 52, is an informal patient with capacity on a ward whose main door is locked to protect detained patients. She asks to go to the shop. What is the correct response?
options: She may leave; staff should open the door for her
She must wait until a doctor agrees to her leave
She cannot leave because the door policy applies
She may leave if an AMHP is told first
C.why: COP15 8.10-8.11: a capable informal patient who has been told about the locked door and agreed to stay is free to leave; the locked door must not become a deprivation of liberty.

whyNot.1: Informal patients do not need medical leave approval to leave the ward.
whyNot.2: A blanket locked door cannot stop an informal patient leaving.
whyNot.3: No AMHP notification is required for an informal patient to leave.

reteach.title: Restrict the risk, not the ward
reteach.question: How do you decide whether a restriction is justified?

blocks.body: Ask: whose risk is this, what is the least restrictive way to manage it, and when will it end? If the answer to the first is 'everyone' because of one incident or low staffing, it is a blanket restriction. Restrict the individual, record why, review it, and keep everyone else's rights intact.

blocks.text: Staff convenience or staffing levels never justify locking areas or banning items for all.

explain.body: Rules applied to all patients without individual risk assessment, such as phone bans, set visiting hours or limits on money or internet. Avoid unless necessary and proportionate for particular individuals, with managers' authorisation and documented impact.

test.q: When can a blanket restriction be implemented under the MHA Code?
options: When the ward manager judges it safer
When a single incident has occurred
When expressly authorised by hospital managers
When most patients agree in a community meeting
test.why: COP15 8.9: no blanket restriction should be implemented unless expressly authorised by the hospital managers under the organisation's policy and governance.

whyNot.0: A ward manager's judgement alone is not authorisation.
whyNot.1: One incident calls for an individual response, not a ward-wide rule.
whyNot.3: Majority agreement does not make a restriction lawful for those who object.

explain.body: Seek consent first and say the person need not consent. Two staff, one the same sex. Explain what is happening, respect privacy, culture and faith, and avoid public areas except in exceptional circumstances.

test.q: Where should a personal search normally take place?
options: In the ward corridor so others can see it
In the dining room after a meal
In a private area that protects dignity
In the nursing office with the door open
test.why: COP15 8.33: searches should ensure maximum dignity and privacy; a search in a public area is justified only in exceptional circumstances.

whyNot.0: A public corridor undermines dignity and privacy.
whyNot.1: A communal room is a public area.
whyNot.3: An open door in a busy office does not protect privacy.

explain.body: For a detained patient who refuses or lacks capacity, keep them separate and observed, contact the RC without delay for any clinical objection, and review before using minimum force. If there is reason to think they have something posing an immediate risk, do not delay.

test.q: A detained patient refuses a search and staff suspect he has a knife he has threatened to use. What does the Code say?
options: Wait for the RC's view before acting
Arrange an MDT meeting for the next day
Do not delay the search; use minimum force
Ask him to sign a disclaimer and leave it
test.why: COP15 8.40-8.41: searches should not be delayed if there is reason to think the person has anything posing an immediate risk; any force must be the minimum necessary.

whyNot.0: Waiting is for situations without immediate danger.
whyNot.1: Delaying a day leaves an immediate risk unmanaged.
whyNot.3: A disclaimer does not manage a threat to others.

explain.body: Assess ligature points and items that could be used to self-harm, involving the person and using the least restrictive measures. Balance this with planned therapeutic risk-taking after a psychosocial assessment, so safety does not crowd out recovery.

test.q: According to NICE NG225, when should therapeutic risk-taking be used for someone who has self-harmed?
options: After a psychosocial assessment
Before any assessment, to build trust
When the risk scale score is low
When the person asks for it
test.why: NG225 1.11.14: therapeutic risk-taking should be used after a psychosocial assessment, with the team, building on strengths and revisited over time.

whyNot.1: NG225 places it after psychosocial assessment, not before.
whyNot.2: NICE advises against using risk scales to make care decisions.
whyNot.3: The person's wishes matter, but the decision follows assessment and team involvement.
